title: 2.1 🌍 GENERAL BACKGROUND TO COLONIALISM
notes:
Colonialism → direct and total dominance of one country by another through foreign state authority; involves subjugation, conquest and exploitation.

Imperialism → policy or belief of using power and influence to rule another nation or people.

📌 Colonialism ↔ closely connected with imperialism.

🏛️ Historical background → colonialism existed since ancient times; Greeks, Romans and Ottomans established colonies.

⛵ From the 16th century → colonialism expanded because advances in navigation enabled Europeans to travel to distant parts of the world.

title: 2.1.1 💱 LEGITIMATE TRADE
notes:
After the Atlantic Slave Trade ended → Europeans increasingly traded with Africa through “legitimate trade” or “legitimate commerce”.

Legitimate trade → commodity trade between Africans and European merchants after abolition of the slave trade.

African exports → mainly raw materials and cash crops.
European exports → manufactured goods.

🔄 Main pattern → African raw materials → European goods.

📌 The shift from human merchandise to tropical commodities increased European competition for African resources and contributed to the race for Africa.

title: 2.1.2 🧭 EUROPEAN EXPLORERS
notes:
Late 18th century–1870s → many European explorers travelled into the interior of Africa.

Two broad groups:

1️⃣ Before the 1850s → generally motivated by scientific inquiry and exploration.

2️⃣ After the 1850s → many were agents of European governments.

📌 Exploration increasingly became connected with European political and colonial expansion.

title: 2.1.3 ✝️ MISSIONARIES AND COLONIAL EXPANSION
notes:
European missionaries → entered Africa to evangelize and introduce Christianity.

They also became associated with → commerce + civilization + colonial administration.

🤝 Missionaries + traders + colonial administrators → often cooperated in the colonial expansion process.

Missionaries → depended on traders for funds and colonial administrators for security.

📌 Late 19th century → missionaries converted less than 1% of non-Muslim Africans outside Ethiopia; some therefore appealed to European governments for assistance.

title: 2.2 💰 MOTIVES OF EUROPEAN COLONIALISM
notes:
The major motives for European colonization of Africa were →

💰 Economic interests
🏛️ Political/strategic interests
⚪ Civilizing Mission & White Man’s Burden
✝️ Religious interests

title: 2.2.1 💰 ECONOMIC MOTIVE
notes:
Industrialization in Europe → factories required large quantities of raw materials and new markets.

🎯 Europeans wanted Africa for:
• Raw materials.
• New market centres.
• Natural resources.
• Agricultural products.
• Minerals.

🌾 Agricultural resources → groundnuts + palm oil + wood + cotton + gum.

⛏️ Mineral resources → rubber + gold + diamonds.

📌 Industrial Revolution → increased European demand for African resources and markets.

title: 2.2.2 🏛️ POLITICAL & STRATEGIC MOTIVE
notes:
European powers → competed for international power and prestige.

Major competitors included → Great Britain + France + Spain and other European powers.

🎯 Strategic goals → control important territories + secure favourable locations + establish military and naval bases.

📌 Colonial possessions became symbols of European power and prestige.

title: 2.2.3 ⚪ CIVILIZING MISSION & 'WHITE MAN’S BURDEN'
notes:
Civilizing Mission → European justification for intervening in and colonizing non-Western peoples.

Europeans claimed they had a mission to spread → civilization + commerce + Christianity.

❗Underlying idea → Europeans were presented as “civilized” while Africans were portrayed as “uncivilized” and inferior.

📜 White Man’s Burden → idea that white people had a supposed responsibility to rule and “civilize” non-white peoples by introducing Western ways.

👤 Rudyard Kipling → wrote the poem “The White Man’s Burden” in 1899.

📌 These ideas were used to justify European colonial domination.

title: 2.2.4 ✝️ RELIGIOUS MOTIVE
notes:
Some missionaries → supported European colonization.

Reason → they believed European political control would create conditions that facilitated missionary activities.

📌 Religion therefore became connected with European colonial expansion.

title: 2.3 🗺️ SCRAMBLE FOR AFRICA
notes:
Before the 1880s → only about 10% of Africa was under foreign rule; most foreign control was limited to coastal areas.

Examples →
• Ottoman/Turkish rule → much of North Africa.
• Oman → Zanzibar.
• Britain → Sierra Leone.
• France → Algeria.
• Boers and Britain → South Africa.
• Portugal → coastal Mozambique and Angola.

🌍 About 90% of Africa → remained free from foreign rule.

🔥 Scramble for Africa → fierce rivalry and rapid European colonial expansion in Africa from the 1880s to the first decade of the 20th century.

📌 1884–1914 → European powers partitioned much of Africa into colonies, protectorates and free-trade areas.

title: 2.3.1 ⚔️ WHY EUROPEANS SUCCESSFULLY PARTITIONED AFRICA
notes:
Two major factors helped European conquest:

1️⃣ Military superiority → European powers possessed professional and well-trained armies and superior weapons.

2️⃣ Lack of African cooperation and solidarity → divisions among African peoples were exploited by Europeans.

📌 European military superiority + African disunity → facilitated rapid colonial conquest.

title: 2.3.2 🤝 METHODS OF COLONIAL OCCUPATION
notes:
European colonial powers used →

📜 Fake/trickery treaties → agreements used to obtain territorial control.

⚔️ Force → military conquest and coercion.

🇪🇹 Wuchale Treaty → textbook example of a trickery treaty between Ethiopia and Italy; discussed in greater detail in another unit.

title: 2.3.3 🏛️ BERLIN CONFERENCE — 1884–1885
notes:
📍 Location → Berlin, Germany.
📅 Period → 1884–1885.
👤 Leader → German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

🌍 Participants → 14 countries, including Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Sweden-Norway, Turkey and USA.

⭐ Major powers → France + Germany + Great Britain + Portugal.

❗Africa → was not invited or represented.

🎯 Main goal → establish rules and discuss the division of Africa among European colonial powers.

📌 The conference marked the real beginning of the large-scale colonization of Africa.

title: 2.3.4 📜 GENERAL ACT OF THE BERLIN CONFERENCE
notes:
The General Act → contained 38 articles and established international guidelines for colonization.

1️⃣ Principle of Effective Occupation → a colonial power needed actual possession through treaties with local leaders, raising its flag, and establishing administration and police forces.

2️⃣ Doctrine of Sphere of Influence → a power taking possession of part of the African coast had to notify the other signatory powers.

3️⃣ End of slavery → conference resolved to end slavery in Africa.

4️⃣ Congo Free State → recognized as the private property of King Leopold II of Belgium.

5️⃣ Free navigation → Niger and Congo rivers were opened to navigation.

📌 Berlin Conference → regulated European competition while Africans had no representation.

title: 2.4 🏛️ COLONIAL POLICIES & ADMINISTRATION
notes:
European colonial governments used different administrative systems according to territory and colonial power.

Main systems →

🏢 Company Rule
🏛️ Direct Rule & Assimilation
🤝 Indirect Rule
🏘️ Settler Rule

📌 Despite differences, colonial systems were generally undemocratic, imposed without African consent, and used divide-and-rule strategies.

title: 2.4.1 🏢 COMPANY RULE
notes:
Company Rule → European governments granted large African territories to private companies for administration.

🎯 Companies → mainly interested in exploiting African natural resources.

📅 Period → approximately 1880s–1924.

🇬🇧 British South Africa Company (B.S.A.C.) → formed in 1887.
👤 John Cecil Rhodes → controlled the company.

B.S.A.C. administered → Nyasaland + Northern Rhodesia + Southern Rhodesia.

⚔️ Methods → force and coercion.

❌ Failure → financial shortages + opposition from Africans and missionaries because of harsh rule.

title: 2.4.2 💎 CECIL RHODES
notes:
Cecil Rhodes → important figure in British colonial expansion in Africa.

1871 → went to South Africa.

By 1889 → controlled about 90% of world diamond production and dominated the gold market.

1890–1896 → Prime Minister of the British Cape Colony.

🎯 Major role → extended British control into other parts of Africa.

title: 2.4.3 🏛️ DIRECT RULE & ASSIMILATION
notes:
Direct Rule → African indigenous rulers and local governments were removed and replaced by European personnel.

African chiefs → often used at lower administrative levels to collect taxes, recruit labour and suppress opposition.

Countries associated with this model → France + Belgium + Germany + Portugal.

🇫🇷 French policy → considered African colonies as part of France.

Assimilation → policy through which Africans receiving French education could potentially become French in culture and status.

It promoted → French language + institutions + laws + customs.

📌 Assimilation → based on the claimed superiority of French culture.

title: 2.4.4 🤝 ASSOCIATION
notes:
Association → another French colonial approach.

🔄 Unlike assimilation → association did not seek identity or complete cultural merging.

🎯 Main idea → cooperation between conquerors and conquered while maintaining differences.

📌 Assimilation → identity/merging with French culture.
📌 Association → cooperation without complete cultural merging.

title: 2.4.5 🤝 INDIRECT RULE
notes:
Indirect Rule → governed colonies through existing indigenous African rulers within the colonial administration.

👤 Architect → Frederick Lugard.

Lugard → used indirect rule in Nigeria and British East Africa.

📖 1922 → Lugard explained the system in “The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa”.

🎯 Reasons → cheaper + considered effective + reduced African resistance.

🇬🇧 British approach → made greater use of African customary law than the French.

⚠️ Negative effect → could aggravate ethnic differences involving language/dialects, dress and religion.

title: 2.4.6 🏘️ SETTLER RULE
notes:
Settler Rule → Europeans settled permanently in African territories and often displaced indigenous Africans.

Major settler areas → South Africa + Southern Rhodesia/Zimbabwe + Northern Rhodesia/Zambia + Angola + Mozambique + South-West Africa/Namibia + Kenya + Algeria.

🌾 Main feature → fertile African land was taken and given to minority white settlers.

⚠️ Effects → harsh and racist administration + Africans became labourers and landless tenants.

🇰🇪 Kenya example → Kikuyu lost ancestral land in the White Highlands and many migrated toward urban centres such as Nairobi for employment.

title: 2.4.7 ⚖️ COMMON FEATURES OF COLONIAL RULE
notes:
Although colonial systems differed, they shared three important features:

❌ Undemocratic → Africans had little or no political participation.

🚫 No consent → colonial rule was usually imposed without African approval.

➗ Divide and Rule → colonial authorities exploited divisions among African communities to strengthen colonial control.

📌 KEY → Undemocratic + imposed without consent + divide and rule.

title: 2.5 ✊ EARLY AFRICAN RESISTANCE MOVEMENTS
notes:
African responses to colonialism → varied from region to region.

✊ Armed resistance → occurred in many parts of Africa.

🕊️ Nonviolent resistance → indigenous press + trade unionism + organized religion + associations + literature + art + mass migration.

📅 Three broad stages:

1️⃣ 1880–1914 → early resistance to colonial conquest.

2️⃣ 1914–1945 → second stage of resistance.

3️⃣ 1950s–1980s → decolonization; national liberation movements aimed at independence.

title: 2.5.1 🌍 RESISTANCE IN WEST AFRICA — AHMADU SEKU
notes:
👤 Ahmadu Seku → prominent leader of the Tukulor Empire.

📅 1830s–1845 → resisted French expansion in West Africa.

Initially → preferred diplomacy rather than armed resistance.

When France violated its promises and expanded territorially → Ahmadu’s forces fought French-Senegalese troops.

❌ Result → Ahmadu's forces were defeated and his empire broke up.

➡️ Ahmadu → exiled to Sokoto, where he died.

📌 French → later allied with Ahmadu's brother to control the region.

title: 2.5.2 ⚔️ RESISTANCE IN WEST AFRICA — SAMORI TURE
notes:
👤 Samori Ture → Muslim leader of the Mandinka Empire.

📅 1882–1898 → conducted prolonged armed resistance against French colonial expansion.

🎯 Achievement → united many people between the source of the Niger and Upper Volta basin under his administration.

⚔️ Army → about 30,000 men.

📍 Area → present-day Guinea + Mali + Côte d’Ivoire.

1900 → French finally captured Samori and exiled him to Gabon.

title: 2.5.3 🛡️ RESISTANCE IN WEST AFRICA — ASANTE
notes:
🇬🇭 Asante Kingdom → resisted British colonial expansion in the Gold Coast.

👑 Leader → Asantehene Prempe.

⚔️ Result → after a bloody war, British forces defeated the resistance.

1900 → Britain established the Gold Coast colony over Ghana.

🇳🇬 Nigeria → British conquest was assisted by:
• Divide-and-rule strategy.
• Superior weapons.
• Recruitment of African troops.

1910 → British conquered the whole of Nigeria.

title: 2.5.4 🌊 EAST AFRICA — MAJI-MAJI UPRISING
notes:
📍 Location → Tanganyika.
📅 1905–1907 → major uprising against German colonial rule.

German policies → high taxation + forced labour + compulsory cotton growing + forced road construction.

👤 Leader/Prophet → Kinjikitle Ngwale.

💧 Maji Maji → sacred water that Ngwale taught would turn enemy bullets into water.

🤝 Spread → involved about 20 ethnic groups.

⚠️ Character → spontaneous uprising with no previous planning or central leadership.

🔥 German response → “scorched earth” policy; villages were destroyed and the rebellion was crushed.

title: 2.5.5 🐄 SOUTH AFRICA — HERERO & NAMA RESISTANCE
notes:
📍 South-West Africa/Namibia → German colonial rule was characterized by land alienation.

🌾 African land → taken and given to German settlers.

Herero and Nama → forced to reduce their grazing land.

1896–1897 → cattle epidemic weakened African communities.

👤 Herero leader → Samuel Maharero.
📅 1904 → Herero rebellion.

👤 Nama leader → Hendrik Witbooi.
📅 1905 → Nama rebellion.

❌ Result → both uprisings were crushed by German forces.

title: 2.5.6 🇪🇬 NORTH AFRICA — URABI RESISTANCE
notes:
📅 1869 → Suez Canal opened, increasing British and French interest in Egypt.

🇬🇧 Britain + 🇫🇷 France → competed for influence in Egypt.

👑 Khedive Ismael Pasha → ruled a weak Egyptian government.

1879 → Britain and France agreed on dual control over Egypt.

1881 → Egyptians revolted against imperialist domination.

👤 Leader → Colonel Urabi Pasha.

1882 → British forces entered Cairo, defeated the revolt and Egypt became a British colony.

title: 2.6 🌍 IMPACTS OF COLONIAL RULE ON AFRICA
notes:
Colonialism affected Africa politically, economically and socially.

Main areas →
🏛️ Political impacts
💰 Economic impacts
👥 Social impacts

📌 Overall → colonial structures were designed mainly to serve European interests and weakened African political, economic and cultural independence.

title: 2.6.1 🏛️ POLITICAL IMPACTS
notes:
❌ Loss of independence and freedom.

🏛️ Indigenous administrations → destroyed or weakened.

🗺️ Artificial boundaries → Europeans created boundaries without approval from local communities.

⚠️ Long-term consequence → colonial boundaries contributed to boundary conflicts among African states after independence.

👥 Colonial borders sometimes:
• grouped previously separate peoples under one government;
• divided existing communities.

📌 Colonial political legacy → weakened indigenous political systems + artificial borders + later conflicts.

title: 2.6.2 💰 ECONOMIC IMPACTS
notes:
Colonial economic policies contributed to African under-development.

🌍 Africa → remained mainly a supplier of raw materials to Europe.

🏭 Manufacturing → Africans were not encouraged or allowed to develop manufacturing industries.

⛏️ Natural resources → heavily exploited by European colonizers.

🌲 Forests → cleared for timber and firewood used for steam trains and railway construction.

🎓 Colonial education → introduced modern education but also contributed to abandonment of some indigenous technological skills and education.

📌 Economic pattern → African raw materials → European industry → African markets for European manufactured goods.

title: 2.6.3 👥 SOCIAL IMPACTS
notes:
🏘️ Community disruption → colonialism changed traditional ways of living.

🚚 Forced relocation → communities were moved to create white settlement areas and large-scale farms.

🦠 Diseases → colonization brought different diseases into African areas.

🐄 Rinderpest → disease introduced by settlers that affected livestock among the Shona of present-day Zimbabwe and Botswana and in North Ethiopia during Kefu Qen.

📌 Social result → displacement + disruption of communities + disease + changes in traditional life.

title: 2.6.4 ⚖️ POSITIVE OUTCOMES MENTIONED
notes:
The textbook also identifies some outcomes associated with colonial rule:

🕊️ Tribal warfare → some conflicts ended following the introduction of colonial administration.

💡 Modern ideas → new ideas and institutions were introduced.

🚂 Transport infrastructure → railways and roads were constructed, particularly to transport raw materials to ports.

📌 Important → these developments were largely designed around colonial economic and administrative interests.

title: 🏆 UNIT 2 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
🌍 COLONIALISM

Colonialism → direct foreign dominance + conquest + exploitation.

Imperialism → use of power/influence to rule another people.

💱 LEGITIMATE TRADE

African raw materials/cash crops ↔ European manufactured goods.

💰 MOTIVES OF COLONIALISM

Economic → raw materials + markets.

Political/Strategic → power + prestige + strategic territories + military/naval bases.

Civilizing Mission → claimed mission to spread civilization, commerce and Christianity.

White Man’s Burden → supposed responsibility to rule/civilize non-white peoples.

Religious → facilitate missionary activities.

🔥 SCRAMBLE FOR AFRICA
1880s–early 20th century → rapid European partition of Africa.

1884–1914 → major period of European colonial expansion.

🏛️ BERLIN CONFERENCE

1884–1885 → Berlin, Germany.

Leader → Otto von Bismarck.

Africa → not represented.

General Act → 38 articles.

Key principles → effective occupation + sphere of influence.

Other agreements → end slavery + Congo Free State recognized as Leopold II’s property + free navigation of Niger and Congo.

🏛️ COLONIAL ADMINISTRATION

Company Rule → private companies administered territories.

Direct Rule → European officials replaced indigenous governments.

Assimilation → extension of French language, laws, institutions and customs.

Association → cooperation rather than cultural merging.

Indirect Rule → indigenous rulers used within colonial administration.

Settler Rule → Europeans settled and took African fertile land.

📌 COMMON FEATURES → undemocratic + imposed without consent + divide and rule.

✊ RESISTANCE
Ahmadu Seku → Tukulor Empire → French.

Samori Ture → Mandinka Empire → French.

Asantehene Prempe → Asante/Gold Coast → British.

Kinjikitle Ngwale → Maji-Maji → German East Africa.

Samuel Maharero → Herero → Germans.

Hendrik Witbooi → Nama → Germans.

Urabi Pasha → Egypt → Britain/France.

📅 KEY RESISTANCE DATES

1830s–1845 → Ahmadu Seku's resistance.

1882–1898 → Samori Ture's armed resistance.

1900 → French captured/exiled Samori.

1900 → British established Gold Coast over Ghana.

1905–1907 → Maji-Maji Uprising.

1904 → Herero rebellion.

1905 → Nama rebellion.

1881 → Urabi-led Egyptian revolt.

1882 → British defeated Urabi revolt; Egypt became British colony.

⚠️ IMPACTS
Political → loss of independence + destruction of indigenous administrations + artificial boundaries + later boundary conflicts.

Economic → raw-material supplier + limited manufacturing + resource exploitation + colonial education effects.

Social → displacement + settler land seizure + disease + disruption of traditional life.

📌 POSITIVE OUTCOMES MENTIONED

End of some tribal warfare + introduction of modern ideas + construction of railways and roads.

🧠 EXAM CONNECTION
Industrial Revolution → demand for raw materials/markets → European competition → Scramble for Africa → Berlin Conference → colonial occupation → African resistance → political/economic/social impacts.
